Using a modified version of CLASS, including the induced particle-mass dependence of recombination, we illustrate the corresponding changes to CMB temperature and linear matter power spectra for benchmark models, without fitting to data. In the strongest benchmarks the fifth force changes the effective gravitational coupling on sub-horizon scales by about one percent, smaller than the accompanying changes to the matter power spectrum and the acoustic scale. For the sign-switching solutions this change is negative over most of cosmic history, so a non-propagating field can weaken rather than strengthen gravitational attraction.

title: MARTA: A "little" black hole hidden in a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at z~3.8
summary: JWST has extended the search for accreting black holes into the high-redshift, low-mass regime. We report a low-mass black hole candidate in MARTA 3887, a clumpy, metal-poor galaxy at $z=3.7694$, combining deep JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy, HST and JWST imaging, and archival VLT/MUSE data. We detect a broad H$α$ component with $L_{\rm Hα,b}=2.35\times10^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and FWHM $=1270^{+260}_{-250}$ km s$^{-1}$, with no [O III] counterpart of comparable width. Under a broad-line-region interpretation, virial calibrations give $\log(M_{\rm BH}/M_\odot)=6.52^{+0.18}_{-0.23}$ and $λ_{\rm Edd}=0.07$, or up to 0.38 for alternative calibrations. The host comprises at least three compact clumps, with $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)=8.16^{+0.09}_{-0.10}$. If stellar photoionization dominates the narrow lines, the gas is highly ionized and metal poor, with $12+\log({\rm O/H})=7.68\pm0.04$ ($\simeq0.10\,Z_\odot$). The inferred $M_{\rm BH}/M_\star=2.3\%$ lies about 2 dex above the extrapolated local relation, suggesting that black-hole growth has outpaced the assembly of the observed host. If growth began only when the first 10% of the observed stellar mass had formed ($t_{10}=92$ Myr ago), a $10^2\,M_\odot$ seed would require a lifetime-mean Eddington ratio $\simeq5.7$; earlier growth or a more massive, e.g. direct-collapse, seed would allow sub-Eddington mean accretion. MUSE reveals extended Ly$α$ emission ($\simeq6.5$-6.9 proper kpc), offset by $+64^{+10}_{-8}$ km s$^{-1}$ from systemic, with a provisional escape fraction of $\simeq0.44$. Together with a Mg II doublet ratio close to the optically thin limit and a high [O III]/[O II] ratio, this makes MARTA 3887 a laboratory to study black-hole growth, stellar assembly, and ionizing-photon escape jointly.

title: EMBER: A Little Red Dot Candidate at $z_{\rm spec}=10.36$ in the Seed Black Hole Era
summary: Little red dots (LRDs) are a newly discovered population that may trace rapidly growing black holes (BHs) and provide a link between seed BHs and luminous active galactic nuclei (AGNs). However, no LRD had previously been spectroscopically confirmed at $z>10$, leaving this earliest phase observationally unexplored. Using JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy from the EMBER program, we measure a spectroscopic redshift of $z_{\rm spec}=10.361^{+0.003}_{-0.002}$ for \target, the highest-redshift LRD candidate known to date. The redshift is constrained by a prominent Ly$α$ break and multiple tentative emission lines, including C\,{\sc iv}\,$λ\lambda1549,1551$ and [O\,{\sc iii}]\,$\lambda4363$ detected at $S/N=3.9$ and $3.6$, respectively. Its extreme NIRCam-MIRI color of $m_{\rm F444W}-m_{\rm F770W}=1.82\pm0.1$, characteristic V-shaped continuum with a turnover near the Balmer limit, and continuum slopes of $β_{\rm UV}=-2.26^{+0.11}_{-0.11}$ and $β_{\rm opt}=1.17^{+0.74}_{-0.70}$ all support its LRD nature. A possible iron complex at $λ_{\rm rest}\sim0.24$--$0.25\,{\rm μm}$ and a possibly high $\log\left([{\rm O\,III]\,\lambda4363/\rm Hγ}\right)=0.17^{+0.24}_{-0.22}$ further support an AGN-like interpretation, as seen in previously known LRDs. Tentative detection of Ly$α$ emission may indicate enhanced Ly$α$ transmission at $z\sim10$. Our findings extend the observational frontier of BH growth into the seed-BH formation era, and upcoming MIRI spectroscopy will further establish the physical nature of the source.

title: First-principles calculations of far-wing absorption in He-broadened CO2 infrared spectra
summary: We report theoretical predictions and modeling of the far-wing absorption of CO2 broadened by He over a wide temperature range (200-1000 K), which are relevant for exoplanet atmosphere studies. Accurate modeling of He-broadened CO2 absorption is essential for opacity calculations used to characterize the composition, structure, and climate of exoplanet atmospheres. In particular, the strong CO2 band at 4.3 mum has been clearly identified in the spectra of several exoplanets observed with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). Requantized classical molecular dynamics simulations were first performed to predict absorption in the far wings of the 4.3 mum band of CO2. The resulting predictions show excellent agreement with available experimental data at room temperature. The theoretical predictions and measured data were then used to parameterize an impact energy-corrected sudden model, which allowed us to accurately reproduce the far-wing absorption of He-broadened CO2 in several infrared spectral regions over the (200-1000) K temperature range. Finally, for applications to exoplanet atmosphere opacity calculations, we derived temperature-dependent chi-factor corrections that account for the sub-Lorentzian behavior of the far wing of the major infrared bands of CO2.

title: Boosted Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving Homogeneous and Non-Homogeneous Lane-Emden Type Equations
summary: The Lane-Emden Equation is a class of nonlinear differential equations commonly used to model phenomena in astrophysics and mathematical physics, such as stellar structure and thermal behavior in polytropic gas spheres. This study presents a novel hybrid framework that integrates Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) with boosting methods to enhance the accuracy and robustness of solutions for Lane-Emden type differential equations. Standard PINNs leverage physical laws encoded within the loss function, but their predictive performance can be constrained by optimization challenges and approximation errors. To address this, we introduce a post-processing boosting stage where the residual errors from the PINN prediction are modeled using some regression algorithms - including LightGBM, Random Forest, XGBoost, and Support Vector Regression (SVR). The outputs from these boosted models are aggregated to generate a corrected, high-fidelity prediction. The proposed methodology is systematically validated through quantitative metrics and comparative analysis against the standard PINN baseline. The results demonstrate that the boosted PINN framework significantly reduces prediction error, and improves generalization, offering a powerful and flexible approach for solving scientific and engineering problems governed by differential equations.

title: From Rock Tumbling to Telescope Mirror Grinding: How Optical Perfection Emerges from Random Motion
summary: When two glass disks are rubbed together by hand with an abrasive between them, their surfaces spontaneously converge to perfectly matching spherical curves, accurate to tens of nanometers. How does such optical precision emerge from an essentially random manual process? Starting from Preston's law of material removal, we derive a first-principles explanation. Symmetries of the grinding stroke imply that planes and spheres are the generic equilibria of the process. Their stability is governed by a hierarchy of timescales: small-scale irregularities decay exponentially on the grinding timescale $T_\text{grind}$, while large-scale deviations from a sphere diffuse away on the longer spherizing timescale $T_\text{sphere} \propto (R_\text{mirror}/R_\text{stroke})^2\, T_\text{grind}$. Gravity and finite disk size destabilize planar surfaces, but for sufficiently short strokes spheres remain stable ($T_\text{deform} \gg T_\text{sphere}$), with only their radius of curvature varying adiabatically. The same framework unifies telescope mirror grinding with everyday phenomena: rock tumbling (explaining why rotary tumbling rounds edges more than vibratory, and why neither produce spheres) and sanding (explaining why small flat surfaces inevitably round). These examples offer an accessible classroom context for stable and unstable equilibria, exponential relaxation, diffusion, multi-timescale analysis, and the emergence of the Laplacian operator from averaging over a local area.

title: Aperture Photometric Accuracy of Point-spread-function-deconvolved Astronomical Images
summary: This paper introduces an improved Richardson--Lucy (RL) framework utilizing negative backfilling (NB) and the novel filtered image deconvolution and noise backfilling (FiDNoBa) algorithm. By integrating a low-pass prefiltering stage---specifically employing a Kalman filter---with the reintegration of filtered-out noise components after RL iterations, we effectively suppress noise artifacts while maintaining rigorous flux integrity. We extensively evaluate our Kalman + RL + NB approach using both numerical simulations and real observational data. Simulations across three regimes demonstrate superior photometric accuracy, reducing the relative mean deviation (RMD) to below 1\% for isolated sources, maintaining high fidelity (RMD $\sim$0.37\%) for blended Sérsic galaxies, and achieving $\sim$5\% RMD in crowded stellar fields while significantly increasing source recovery rates compared to traditional point-spread function photometry. Crucially, we validate the practical efficacy of FiDNoBa on real space-based (JWST/NIRCam) and ground-based (Very Large Telescope Survey Telescope OmegaCAM) images. The results confirm that our method reliably handles complex instrumental signatures, such as the extended wings of the STPSF, mitigating the severe ringing artifacts typical of traditional RL deconvolution while ensuring highly stable aperture photometry in practical survey processing.

title: An Unusually Clumpy Ultra-Diffuse Galaxy in the Coma Cluster: A Missing Link for Globular Cluster Formation?
summary: We present a study of Coma-B122, an unusually clumpy star-forming ultra-diffuse galaxy (UDG) in the Coma cluster outskirts, using deep Keck Cosmic Web Imager integral-field spectroscopy and Subaru Hyper Suprime-Cam imaging. B122 hosts $\sim10$ luminous star-forming clumps contributing $\sim25$% of its luminosity and $\sim7$% of its stellar mass, with typical clump masses of $\sim10^6\ M_\odot$ comparable to the most massive super star clusters known in nearby starbursting dwarfs. The clumps form a distinctive ring configuration $\sim2$ kpc from the center. Full-spectrum fitting shows that $\sim12.5$% of the diffuse body's stellar mass formed during an extended episode of enhanced star formation over the past $\sim300$ Myr, within which all the clumps assembled. B122 shows evidence of weak ram-pressure stripping (RPS), including a diffuse light distribution truncated on the side facing the Coma center and extended to the opposite side, along with an asymmetric H I velocity profile. Its ordered stellar and ionized-gas rotation, cold gas fraction, and phase-space position are consistent with an early stage of infall. Spatial variations in clump star formation histories and gas-phase abundances further indicate that RPS-driven metal-poor gas inflow may have triggered and sustained the recent star formation. B122 may offer a rare present-day view of how UDGs assemble their globular cluster (GC) systems during cluster infall, although it remains uncertain if the clumps could survive as GCs. Future observations with higher spatial resolution and of more analogs are important to provide a complete picture of the formation and evolution of clumpy low-surface-brightness dwarf galaxies.

title: Choosing a generator for streaming Gaussian noise in gravitational-wave mock data: accuracy, cost and reproducibility
summary: Mock data challenges need long stretches of colored Gaussian noise with a prescribed spectrum. The candidates are the crossfade of independently drawn windows that the standard gravitational-wave libraries implement, overlap-save finite-impulse-response filtering, autoregressive and autoregressive moving-average (ARMA) models, and the reproducible filter of PyCBC. One measure ranks them all: the covariance error against the target over the analysis band, evaluated from each generator's algebra; generated noise only checks the implementations. We also measure throughput, retained state and the cost of bit-exact regeneration. With the target continued smoothly below the band, the crossfade with windows of 256 s or more reaches an error below $10^{-3}$ on all eleven detector curves as tabulated, at about 4.7 million samples per second from a state of a few hundred bytes. An overlap-save filter is faster but needs tens of thousands of taps for an error of a few percent, and no tested autoregressive or ARMA configuration lies on the accuracy--throughput fronts. An error of $10^{-3}$ needs a window of 8 to 235 s, longest on the design curves with narrow lines, where it also depends on the tabulation. With the target cut at the band edge, as current generators do by default, every method has an error above one half on the projected Advanced LIGO (aLIGO) O4 curve, and the crossfade on five other curves. The crossfade is cyclostationary. With the continued target, its cyclic part is the larger part of the error only at 8 s, on the aLIGO O4 and the Virgo and KAGRA design curves, and stays within a factor of two of the stationary part on the aLIGO O3 and the Virgo and KAGRA design curves. We recommend the crossfade with a window from the table of detector curves, and a smooth continuation of the target below the band.

title: Physically Motivated Stellar Populations for Galaxies at Cosmic Dawn with a Temperature-Dependent IMF
summary: The first few years of James Webb Space Telescope observations have identified previously undetected galaxies at $z>12$ and provided new constraints on galaxies at $z>8$. Many of these objects have stellar masses that are difficult to reconcile with $Λ$CDM, inferred from models not calibrated for the high-redshift Universe. This necessitates new, more astrophysically plausible stellar population models for estimating stellar masses of galaxies at cosmic dawn. We introduce a simple stellar population (SSP) library, Simple Stellar Populations with Temperature (SSPT), computed using a temperature-dependent stellar initial mass function and its implementation in the public code CIGALE. When used in a configuration designed for high-redshift galaxies that requires young stellar population ages, the new models predict stellar masses that are ~0.3-0.5 dex lower than estimates from similar CIGALE analyses using models calibrated to the local Universe, and nearly 2 dex lower than estimates from analyses using other codes and softer constraints on stellar ages. Application of these physically motivated stellar populations suggests that stellar masses of early star-forming galaxies are not in tension with $Λ$CDM, and that galaxy formation from virialized halos remains a reasonable hypothesis at the highest redshifts. The SSPT SSPs and their CIGALE implementation are released publicly.

title: Deconvolved IXPE Polarization Maps of the Crab Nebula in a Maximum-a-Posteriori Framework
summary: We analyze the first IXPE observation of the Crab Nebula using a polarization-resolved deconvolution method based on maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation. The method reconstructs the polarization-resolved intensity map as a three-dimensional distribution in sky-position and polarization-angle spaces, using an instrumental response that depends on the incident direction and polarization angle of X-ray photons. We apply the method to the IXPE data in the 2-8~keV band and compare the result with that obtained using the basic analysis. Our result shows sharper spatial structure, making the jet shape more clearly identifiable than that in the basic analysis. The reconstructed image shows a statistically significant tendency for the magnetic-field orientation to be perpendicular to the intensity-gradient orientation in the jet region. Although these results are obtained by using a simplified response where systematic uncertainty remains, they demonstrate that our MAP-based deconvolution can improve the interpretability of IXPE polarization maps for nebular sources.

title: J-PAS: Exploring the connection between local environment and the triggering of bursty star formation in Extreme Emission Line Galaxies
summary: [Abridged]Extreme Emission Line Galaxies (EELGs) are compact, low-mass systems undergoing intense bursts of star formation, whose physical conditions resemble those of galaxies in the early Universe. We characterise the local environment of EELGs identified in the J-PAS survey to determine whether their extreme properties are associated with the presence of nearby companions, as expected if galaxy-galaxy interactions were the main trigger of the burst. We analyse 917 EELGs from the J-PAS internal data release at $0.03 \lesssim z \lesssim 0.9$ over $\sim$30 deg$^2$. We use the Pair Probability Function formalism, based on the full photometric redshift probability distributions, to identify companions within projected separations up to 200 kpc and velocity differences up to 500 km s$^{-1}$. Stellar masses, star formation rates, dust attenuation, and metallicity estimates were derived for the EELGs and their companions through SED fitting with CIGALE, and Monte Carlo simulations were used to correct for projection and completeness effects. The average pair fraction of the EELGs is $f_\mathrm{pair} = 0.162^{+0.048}_{-0.033}$, indicating that only $\sim$16% of the sample has detectable companions, a value lower than the observed average for other star-forming galaxies within the adopted limits. When detected within the sensitivity and stellar-mass completeness limits of J-PAS, companions tend to be more massive and to show higher SED-based metallicity estimates than the EELGs, suggesting that the latter are typically the low-mass components of asymmetric pairs. However, lower-mass companions below these limits may remain undetected. No statistically significant correlation is found between the equivalent widths of the [OIII]$λ$5007, H$β$, and H$α$ emission lines and the projected separation to the detected companions within the J-PAS limits.

title: An Empirical Temperature Relation for Chemical Abundances in AGN
summary: We present for the very first time the empirical temperature structure of the narrow line region (NLR) clouds of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) based on a sample of [N II] and [O III] auroral line measurements. The scaling of Te([N II]) with Te([O III]), expressed as the t2-t3 relation, is key to deriving accurate chemical abundances, in AGNs and other line-emitting nebulae, particularly when only one auroral line is observed. Here, we provide the first robust empirical description of t2-t3 for AGNs: t2(10^4 K)=1.285*t3(10^4 K)+0.799. We find substantial changes in 12+log(O/H) when compared to other t2-t3 calibrations when using the direct, or Te, method with only the [O III] 4363 auroral line. We find that adopting our t2-t3 most accurately recovers the fully direct method 12+log(O/H). To interpret the physical mechanisms behind the AGN t2-t3, we compare the observed distribution of [N II] 6584/5755 and [O III] 5007/4363 flux ratios to a variety of ionization model predictions. We find evidence for power law density gradients, pressure stratification, and (sometimes significant) contributions from astrophysical shocks driving much of the dispersion on these flux ratios while metal cooling dominates the primary shape of the distribution. With more accurate t2-t3 and 12+log(O/H), the properties of the interstellar medium photoionized by AGN can be better characterized and understood across a wide range of cosmic time and may bring better context for novel observations at z>6 with JWST, with implications for understanding chemical enrichment in the earliest stages of galaxy evolution.

title: Episodic Star Formation - II. The Origin of the Fundamental Metallicity Relation
summary: The Fundamental Metallicity Relation (FMR) extends the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) by including star formation rate (SFR) as a third parameter. At fixed stellar mass, galaxies with higher SFRs tend to have lower gas-phase metallicities. We investigate the physical origin of the FMR in the context of episodic star formation (Gui et al. 2026, paper I of this series) by tracing the evolution histories of 8,979 central star-forming galaxies selected at $z=0$ in TNG100 back to $z=1$. We find that the overall MZR scatter at $z=0$ ($\sim0.11$ dex) comprises both long-lived differences among galaxies ($\sim0.09$ dex) and temporal fluctuations within individual galaxies ($\sim 0.07$ dex). The galaxy-to-galaxy component shows an anticorrelation between SFR and gas-phase metallicity, as shown by the observed FMR. As for the consequence from temporal fluctuation, we track individual histories and stack the upward and downward SFR phases of a refined sample. Time-shift analysis and stacked histories show a well-behaved sequence in which the cold non-star-forming gas reservoir increases (decreases) first, followed by a decrease (increase) in gas-phase metallicity and then a rise (decline) in SFR. This ordering is consistent with a physical scenario where metal-poor gas first replenishes the cold reservoir and dilutes the gas before SFR rises to the peak, followed by feedback-driven gas heating/removal, resulting in a shift in metallicity from dilution to enrichment as SFR decreases towards the valley. This naturally explains the anticorrelation between the SFR and gas-phase metallicities as indicated by the observed FMR.

title: Targeting the future of spectroscopic galaxy surveys -- A cosmological study case with the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope
summary: The next generation of Stage-V spectroscopic surveys are designed to measure hundreds of millions of galaxy and quasar spectra, extending precision large-scale-structure cosmology to redshifts and volumes well beyond the reach of current Stage-IV facilities. Realising this potential requires revisiting the target selection strategies and designing them explicitly around the depth, multiplexing, and survey time of the new instruments, rather than a direct extrapolation of existing recipes. This work develops and characterises new strategies for the Wide-field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST), a proposed 12-metre, highly multiplexed facility expected to operate in the 2040s. Using deep multi-band photometry, including COSMOS-field data from CLAUDS and HSC, we revisit low-redshift $z<1.6$ tracer selection of SDSS, BOSS/eBOSS, DESI and 4MOST-CRS -- Bright Galaxies, Luminous Red Galaxies, Emission Line Galaxies and quasars -- to photometric depth achievable in the WST era, and introduce a purely magnitude-limited sample (MagMax) exploiting three-dimensional colour-colour star-galaxy separation, and a set of Lyman-Break Galaxy dropout samples extending target selection to $z>2$. Using Fisher-matrix forecasts, we showcase the constraining power of a WST-like cosmological survey on BAO distance parameters $α_\parallel$ and $α_\perp$, the growth rate $f$, the evolving dark energy equation $w_0w_a$, the local-type primordial non-Gaussianity $f_{\rm NL}^{\rm loc}$, and the sum of the neutrino mass $Σm_ν$. The main outcome of this work is an optimisation framework that directly links instrumental capabilities and observing time to cosmological constraining power, providing a science-driven template applicable to the design of future generations of Stage-V spectroscopic surveys.

title: Simulating winds in the Galactic centre. II. Observational biases on HI clouds and a multi-wavelength comparison
summary: High-velocity neutral hydrogen (HI) clouds found up to several kiloparsecs above the Galactic centre (GC) provide some of the most direct evidence for a nuclear wind in the Milky Way, yet the properties inferred for these clouds are influenced by how they are observed. Starting from a magnetohydrodynamical simulation in which supernova feedback drives a multiphase nuclear outflow, we generate mock HI observations matched to the angular resolution and sensitivity of Green Bank Telescope (GBT) surveys of the GC and analyse them in the same way as the real data. We find that observational effects substantially reshape the cloud population: beam smearing makes clouds appear larger, rounder and more diffuse, while noise erases faint clouds and strips low-density gas from the others. These effects combined, together with confusion with foreground disk emission, prevent the detection of more than 80% of the clouds (up to 95% during more quiescent phases), while those detected appear less massive, less turbulent and less elongated, with column densities underestimated by a factor of two; only their velocities are reliably recovered. Once these effects are included, the simulated clouds broadly reproduce the properties and sky distribution of the GBT population, but lack the fastest (> 250 km/s ) and highest-latitude (b > 10° ) clouds. Mock UV absorption and soft X-ray observations support this picture, with warm-ionized gas column densities at the low end of the observed range and X-ray emission measures too low at b > 10° . Our results imply that the true GC cloud population is more numerous, massive, turbulent and elongated than observed, and that fully reproducing observations may require a stronger recent starburst or additional feedback.

title: Chemical abundances of a Galactic Centre ejecta discovered in DESI
summary: Chemical abundances in the Galactic Centre (GC) are challenging to measure because of high extinction, crowding, and distance, and are typically limited to the brightest AGB and M giants observed in the near-infrared. In contrast, hypervelocity stars (HVSs) ejected from the GC by Sgr A* carry their natal composition into accessible regions such as the Milky Way halo, making them unique probes of GC chemistry. We present high-resolution optical Magellan/MIKE spectroscopy of DESI-312, a bound HVS candidate in the halo with super-solar metallicity ($[\mathrm{Fe/H}]=0.2\pm0.1$). This sets it apart from accreted halo populations on radial orbits and is most naturally explained by GC formation and Hills-mechanism ejection. Updated isochrone fits give an age of 7.4-11.3 Gyr; together with its metallicity and kinematics, this strengthens the case for a GC origin. Korg and Turbospectrum spectral synthesis yields $[\mathrm{X/Fe}]$ for 22 elements, plus Li from an independent line-by-line NLTE analysis. As DESI-312 is near the main sequence, its C, N, and O abundances are unaltered by dredge-up; to our knowledge, these are the first such measurements of unevolved GC material. Its abundance pattern lies where the nuclear star cluster (NSC), nuclear stellar disc (NSD), and inner-bulge sequences overlap, with a Na enhancement ($[\mathrm{Na/Fe}]=+0.16^{+0.03}_{-0.04}$) more modest than in NSC giants of similar metallicity. Chemistry alone thus cannot identify its progenitor; we nevertheless favour the NSC, given its large reservoir of old, metal-rich stars and the star's kinematics. Alongside WINERED-HVS1 and the S-star S0-6/S10, whose abundances point to different progenitors, this tentatively suggests multiple progenitor populations for the S-star cluster. DESI-312 is a test case for sampling GC chemistry with ejected dwarfs at optical wavelengths, complementing near-infrared studies of giants.

title: On the Role of Gravity in Supercooled Phase Transitions
summary: Theories with radiative mass generation and radiative symmetry breaking (RSB) lead to first-order phase transitions (FOPTs) and the production of gravitational waves (GWs) as well as primordial black holes if supercooling lasts long enough. Here we investigate the role of gravity in supercooled FOPTs that occur in the RSB scenario. We use a model-independent approach that is valid when a quantity (which we explicitly determine and is computable once the model is specified) is small enough. Eventually, the curvature of spacetime becomes relevant if the FOPT does not complete in the case in which gravity is ignored. We also include the effect on the FOPT of the non-minimal couplings with coefficients of zero mass dimension. Depending on such non-minimal couplings, gravity can enhance or reduce the region of parameter space where the phase transition completes. Observable consequences of the role of gravity on the FOPT that can be probed by current and future GW detectors are then worked out and we explore the possibility that the background of GWs detected by pulsar timing arrays is produced by FOPTs in the RSB scenario. We also estimate the number of e-folds that elapse when the field playing the role of the order parameter is trapped in the false vacuum, which provides important information for cosmology.

title: See you again: an $80^\circ$ NGC~5466 stellar stream and its constraints on the Galactic dark halo mass
summary: Using \textit{Gaia} Data Release 3 combined with Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Legacy Imaging Survey Data Release 9 and Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System Data Release 2, we apply a modified matched filter method to obtain a weighted stellar map in the surrounding of the globular cluster NGC~5466. Our results support that the tidal stream of NGC~5466 extends around $80^\circ$ on the sky, and the leading tail seemingly exhibits an upward deviation in the range of $180^\circ \lesssim α\lesssim 190^\circ$, which supports previous claim that the Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) may have caused dynamical perturbations to the stream. Based on the 308 highly-weighted member candidates of the NGC~5466 stream, we try to measure the mass distribution of the Milky Way dark matter halo along with the mass of LMC. By comparing the observed stream candidate members to a series of model streams generated under different potential parameters, we obtain the posterior distributions of the parameters: the circular velocity at the solar radius $V_{\rm c} = 239.56^{+1.46}_{-1.44}\ \mathrm{km\ s^{-1}}$, the density flattening of the halo $q = 1.08^{+0.07}_{-0.07}$, the scale radius of the halo density profile $r_s = 12.97^{+3.02}_{-2.18}\ \mathrm{kpc}$ and the total mass of the LMC $M_{\rm LMC} = 9.63^{+1.89}_{-2.00}\times 10^{10}$ $\mathrm{M_\odot}$. The enclosed mass of the Milky Way within the stream apocenter radius of $\sim$ 50 kpc is calculated as $M_{\rm MW}(<50~\mathrm{kpc}) = 4.59^{+0.48}_{-0.37} \times 10^{11}$ $\mathrm{M_\odot}$.

title: Stars Can Quench Superradiance Around Supermassive Black Holes
summary: Light scalar fields trigger an instability around rotating black holes which drives the rapid growth of high-density bound states on astrophysically short timescales---a phenomenon known as black hole superradiance. This process is usually tacitly assumed to happen independent of the local environment. Around supermassive black holes, however, orbiting stars and compact objects act as a perturbation that drains energy from the cloud, potentially preventing its formation altogether. In this work, we quantify under what conditions this happens, focusing on bound-free state transitions. We first compute the rate of energy dissipation due to gravitational interactions, finding that the superradiance growth rate almost always dominates the environmental depletion. The two rates are, however, close enough that the conclusion could be overturned once bound-bound transitions are included. Also, the environment dissipates the cloud faster than gravitational-wave emission, implying that stellar environments must be accounted for in a variety of indirect search strategies. We then investigate the impact of the scalar's quadratic couplings to nucleons and electromagnetism, showing that these interactions can greatly enhance energy dissipation, preventing the cloud's formation. This work highlights the importance of accounting for the local environment in studies of superradiance around intermediate and supermassive black holes.

title: Detection of the Galaxy--Galaxy--Temperature Skewed Bispectrum
summary: We present the first measurement of the galaxy--galaxy--temperature skewed bispectrum, obtained by cross-correlating the squared, filtered unWISE galaxy overdensity with \textit{Planck} maps at 100, 143, 217, and 353~GHz. The signal is detected with high significance in all four channels. Its frequency dependence reveals contributions from hot gas through the thermal Sunyaev--Zel'dovich (tSZ) effect and from dust through the cosmic infrared background (CIB). With the galaxy occupation fixed, our halo-model fits favor higher integrated pressure and peak star-formation efficiency for the galaxy--temperature cross-spectra than for the skewed bispectrum. Comparisons with component-separated tSZ and CIB maps from the same \textit{Planck} observations indicate that this mismatch is not confined to the frequency-map fits. This difference motivates testing more flexible descriptions of gas pressure, CIB emission, and galaxy occupation. In particular, it could point to a mass dependence of the gas-pressure profile that our model does not fully capture. By giving greater weight to massive halos that host many galaxy pairs, the skewed bispectrum provides a complementary test of these descriptions, using information beyond two-point statistics at a comparable computational cost.

title: Nonlinear gauge maps and the structure of Goldstone loops in canonical inflation
summary: We clarify the nonlinear relation between the spatially flat scalar and Goldstone descriptions of canonical single-field inflation. An exact clock map shows how potential interactions are reorganized into derivative Goldstone interactions. A change of slicing further connects their dilation symmetry to its comoving realization. We then study the Goldstone two-point function at one loop in the decoupling limit. Using identities derived from the general mode equation, we reveal how seemingly independent loop contributions combine and their non-boundary parts cancel once the associated counterterms are included. This reduction requires no explicit mode-function solution. The leading adiabatic long-mode response reduces to a total derivative in loop momentum, which requires an additional regularization prescription.

title: A Physics Informed Neural Network Approach to Decipher Environmental Confinement of Molecular Clouds in the Third Galactic Quadrant
summary: Recent high-sensitivity and high-resolution surveys of the Third Galactic Quadrant [$219.75 \leq l \leq 229.75$ and $-5.25 \leq b \leq 5.25$], such as the Milky Way Imaging Scroll Painting ( MWISP) survey, have revealed a significant population of molecular clouds (MCs) that appear virially unbound ($α_{vir} > 2$) according to traditional isolated MC models. However, these apparently unstable cloud structures are actually found long-lived and actively undertaking star formation. This inconsistency presents a Virial Paradox. In the present work, we employ a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) to address this discrepancy by re-evaluating the stability of 2,091 MCs . Unlike traditional machine learning, our PINN model embeds the complete Eulerian Virial Theorem including external surface pressure support ($P_{ext}$) directly into the network's loss function. This model autonomously discovers a global Galactic pressure field that scales inversely with vertical height ($|z|$) and Galactocentric radius ($R_{GC}$), consistent with the properties of the Galactic Flare. By incorporating this AI-derived pressure support, we demonstrate a dramatic shift in the stability census: 99.9\% of previously thought unbound clouds are found to be in a state of pressure confined equilibrium ($α_{AI} \leq 2$). Furthermore, we find a robust log-log correlation ($R = 0.64$) between our corrected stability parameter and the star formation rate (SFR). This correlation provides independent physical validation that environmental confinement is a primary regulator of star forming efficiency in the outer Galaxy.

title: What can strong lensing recover in edge-on disc galaxies? A mock study based on TNG50 simulations
summary: Strong gravitational lensing tightly constrains the projected mass within the Einstein aperture, but what else imaging alone can recover for edge-on disc lenses remains untested against known truth. We construct HST/ACS-like mock observations of 35 edge-on TNG50 disc galaxies selected to resemble lenses from the Sloan WFC Edge-on Late-type Lens Survey (SWELLS), and fit them with a five-stage Source-Light-and-Mass workflow in PyAutoLens; the final model represents the lens mass distribution by scaling the Multi-Gaussian Expansion (MGE) foreground-light template with a global mass-to-light ratio and adding a spherical NFW halo. Decomposed fits succeed for 21 of the 35 systems; in the other 14, coherent MGE lens-light residuals prevent reliable modelling. For the successful subset, the Einstein radius and the total aperture mass are recovered with normalised median absolute deviation (NMAD) scatters of 0.3% and 0.7%. The global projected mass-weighted slope has an NMAD scatter of 10.3%, smaller than that of the mass-sheet-invariant reduced deflection curvature $ξ$ (11.4%) and well below that of the local slope (40.7%), while the stellar and dark-matter aperture masses scatter by 15.1% and 108.8%. A 35-system true-light diagnostic using the exact input light gives component-mass scatters of 0.8% and 6.3%. Under these controlled assumptions, imaging constrains Einstein-scale total mass and global radial structure more reliably than local radial structure or the stellar-dark-matter decomposition.

title: Kinematic analysis of the TNG50 Milky Way and Andromeda analogues
summary: We investigate whether Ogorodnikov-Milne (O-M) parameters can serve as kinematic tracers of spiral structure in four Milky Way- and Andromeda-like disc galaxies from the TNG50-1 simulation at z=0. Stellar particles are analysed in disc-aligned reference frames, with velocities referenced to the mass-weighted mean stellar velocity within one stellar half-mass radius. Local O-M fits on a regular grid yield centroid velocities and the components of the velocity-gradient tensor, characterising local deformation and rotation. We compare their spatial distributions with stellar surface-density and relative overdensity maps and examine the influence of parameter uncertainties. The galaxies exhibit diverse coherent kinematic patterns. Features selected using the generalised Oort constants A, B, and C+K display partial correspondence with stellar overdensities, depending on the galaxy and the adopted centroid-selection criteria. For TNG50-456326, a galaxy-specific selection enables us to fit four logarithmic spiral branches and determine their geometrical parameters. Their morphology suggests two principal arms and two secondary branches. We compare the fitted spirals with stellar- and gas-mass overdensity and radial velocity maps and examine the spatial relationship between the identified stellar structures and the gas distribution. Qualitative similarities to the morphology and kinematic patterns of the Milky Way make TNG50-456326 a promising candidate for further investigation as a kinematic analogue. Our results support the use of local O-M parameters as complementary diagnostics of non-axisymmetric disc structure, while highlighting the need for galaxy-specific selection criteria.

title: Solving the Mystery of the Electron Radiation Belt at Uranus: Leveraging Knowledge of Earth's Radiation Belts in a Re-Examination of Voyager 2 Observations
summary: Voyager 2 provided the only direct measurement of the radiation environment at Uranus and established the well-accepted characterization of a system with a weaker ion radiation belt and surprisingly intense electron radiation belt. Recent re-analysis of the flyby, however, suggests that these observations were not taken during normal solar wind conditions, and instead occurred while a large solar wind transient, a corotating interaction region, was passing over the system. With this context, this study compares the Voyager 2 observations to a similar event observed at Earth. This comparative approach, along with an expanded contextual interpretation of the Voyager 2 flyby, suggests that solar wind-magnetospheric interactions at Uranus may have driven enhanced lower band chorus wave emissions capable of accelerating electrons to relativistic energies. This motivates new, more expansive questions to be explored at Uranus and highlights the need for a Uranus orbiter mission.

title: The nucleon is not a hard sphere: screening fifth forces with Skyrmions
summary: Laboratory searches for chameleon and symmetron fifth forces increasingly rely on individual nucleons as sources or probes, but model them as uniform spheres. Motivated by the Skyrme picture, we instead consider a nucleon profile with a constant-density core and an $r^{-6}$ pion tail, together with its exponential truncation at the physical pion mass. We derive analytic screening charges for the uniform sphere and the $r^{-6}$ profile, and extend the comparison to the exponential truncation at the physical pion mass using numerical solutions. Because the outer tail is too dilute to be screened at any coupling strength, the $r^{-6}$ tail produces a power-law enhancement over the sphere charge in strong screening, and the exponential tail has a weaker, logarithmic enhancement. Propagating this difference through the published analyses, nucleon-sourced exclusion regions extend systematically further into the strongly coupled regime. For example, symmetron constraints from neutron interferometry at $μ=1\,\mathrm{keV}$ reach maximal self-couplings about $1.4$ orders of magnitude higher than for a uniform-sphere neutron ($3.0$ orders of magnitude in the chiral limit),and at the dark-energy scale the hydrogen $1s$--$2s$ chameleon bound reaches couplings $1.8$ orders of magnitude weaker than for a uniform-sphere proton ($2.4$ in the chiral limit), overtaking the muonium bound.

title: The L1157 filament as traced in HNCO by the LMT
summary: Context. The L1157 outflow is a prototype of chemically active outflows where to look for molecular species linked to complex chemistry. Aims. With the aim of imaging the large (parsec) scale structure of key prebiotic molecules, we have mapped the whole blue-lobe of the L1157 outflow with the Large Millimeter Telescope (LMT), proving the potential of this facility to detect weak and extended molecular emission. Methods. Isocyanic acid, HNCO, an important precursor of complex chemistry, was chosen to be observed in its (4_0,4-3_0-3) transition at 87.925 GHz with the SEQUOIA focal-plane array, covering an area of 3x3 arcmin2 centered at the position of the main shock L1157-B1, which included a large portion of the vicinity of the protostellar region. Results. The HNCO emission was detected not only from the outflow but it also was found tracing a structure of about 0.3 pc in length, corresponding to the filament from which the protostellar system was born. Conclusions. The HNCO molecule was found to be a tracer of the densest part of filaments in molecular clouds, and given its importance in the formation of more complex molecules, its presence in the cold, quiescent filamentary gas indicates that the building blocks of complex chemistry are already well established in stages prior to protostellar warming or shocks. By allowing the detection of structures related with the filament, these observations proved the LMT potentialities to map weak and extended components in molecular clouds.

title: Shear Mapping in Python (SMPy): Modular, Extensible, and Accessible Dark Matter Mapping
summary: Understanding the Universe's large-scale distribution of dark matter is a central objective in the era of precision cosmology. A key technique for the study of dark matter is weak gravitational lensing: a phenomenon where light from distant galaxies is sheared as it passes through the gravitational field of a massive object, like a galaxy cluster. This shear, which manifests as a slight (weak) distortion of shapes over thousands of galaxies, allows astrophysicists to infer the distribution of total matter, including both luminous and dark matter. Obtaining a mass distribution from a catalog of galaxy shears involves reconstructing the convergence ($κ$), the projected surface mass density divided by the critical surface density for the lens-source system. The Shear Mapping in Python (SMPy) package provides a standardized, well-documented, and open-source solution for creating convergence maps from weak lensing galaxy shear measurements. SMPy implements three mapping methods: the classic Kaiser-Squires inversion, aperture mass mapping, and, to our knowledge, the first publicly available implementation of the full KS+ algorithm, which corrects for missing data, field borders, and reduced shear. SMPy was initially developed to support the Superpressure Balloon-borne Imaging Telescope (SuperBIT) and has since evolved into a general-purpose tool suitable for analyzing the weak lensing data from cosmological surveys.

title: Euclid Quick Data Release (Q1). Mass-to-light ratio of elliptical galaxies: constraints from strong lensing
summary: Mass is among the most fundamental properties describing a galaxy. The relation between the luminosity and the total mass of a galaxy contains information on the efficiency of the star formation process and on the distribution of dark matter. We used strong gravitational lensing data from the Euclid Quick Data Release 1 (Q1) to constrain the total mass enclosed within an aperture of $5\,h^{-1}$kpc, $M_5$, of elliptical galaxies. Our analysis is based on a sample of 95 lenses, which we built by ensuring that their selection function is reproducible. This enabled us to correct our inference for selection effects. The average $\log_{10}{(M_5\,h\,M_\odot^{-1})}$ for a galaxy with an $r$-band luminosity of $10^{10.7}L_{\odot}\,h^{-2}$ at $z=0.5$ is $11.30\pm0.02$. The mass $M_5$ scales with luminosity to the power $β_\mathrm{L}=0.71\pm0.07$, and decreases with increasing redshift at fixed luminosity. Assuming a scenario in which galaxies grow by mergers and stellar populations evolve passively, these correlations imply that $M_5$ increases with time for individual galaxies. These measurements provide a useful benchmark for testing models of galaxy structure and evolution that make predictions on the distribution of total mass on the scales of $5\,h^{-1}$kpc.

title: Intranight optical monitoring of eight quasars with superluminal jets and low optical polarization: Probing the mechanism of rapid flux variability
summary: Intranight optical variability (INOV) of blazars whose emission arises predominantly from a relativistic jet, has been widely linked to a combination of two key observational diagnostics: the fractional optical polarization ($P_{opt}$) and the Doppler boost arising from relativistic beaming of the jet's emission. To discern which of these two factors plays the dominant role, we investigate INOV of a well-defined representative sample of 8 flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs, which are `low-synchrotron-peaked' blazars) whose jets exhibit a low degree of polarization ($P_{opt}$ < 3$\%$) but a large superluminal motion with c$β_{app}$ = 5c $-$ 31c (median = 10c). We report sensitive optical monitoring of these 8 `low-polarization superluminal quasars' (LPSQs) using a 1.3-metre telescope, in 20 sessions of minimum 3-hour duration. These data were supplemented with similarly high-quality monitoring data/results available in the literature for this sample, thus adding another 19 sessions. Duty cycle (DC) of strong INOV (amplitude $ψ> 5\%$) is found to be zero, applying the normally used $F_η$ test, and $\sim 7\%$ using the more powerful `enhanced $F$-test'. The small DC, despite the strong Doppler boost expected from the observed high superluminality, shows that strong INOV is much rarer among LPSQs, compared to high-polarization quasars, for which DC $(ψ> 5\%$) is found to be around 30%, even using the $F_η$ test. This provides the first compelling evidence that optical polarization is the primary diagnostic of INOV, while relativistic beaming plays a supportive role. Possible implications for the proposed mechanisms for INOV are pointed out.

title: A Supermagnified Little Red Dot with a Resolved Host
summary: Little red dots (LRDs) are an intriguing new class of sources in the early universe discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) characterized by V-shaped spectra and extremely compact sizes. Their underlying mechanisms still remain the subject of ongoing debate. We present JWST observations of a gravitationally lensed LRD nicknamed "Best Friend" at $z_{\rm spec} = 8.297\pm0.002$. Its high magnification factor of $μ= 36^{+8}_{-12}$ makes it the highest magnified LRD reported to date and unveils both the resolved structure of its host and a central engine less than 7 pc in size. The spectrum of the central engine, in which broad lines are not detected, possibly owing to the limited S/N and spectral resolution, is better interpreted as black hole activity rather than a dense star cluster. The latter cannot be fully excluded, but if true, the resulting lower limit on stellar density would be $>1.25^{+0.4}_{-0.3}\cdot10^6 \mathrm{M_{\odot}/pc}^2$, which is around 2 orders of magnitude higher than stellar densities of typical clusters at high-z. By performing a spatially resolved analysis of NIRCam photometry and NIRSpec/PRISM spectroscopy, we find that the host stellar mass is $\log(M_\star/M_{\odot}) = 7.3^{+0.2}_{-0.8}$. Best Friend demonstrates the power of lensing to reveal the morphologies of LRDs.

title: Galaxy cluster thermodynamics at z=1.7: Resolved tSZ and X-ray analysis of CL J0459.6-4946
summary: Measurements of the entropy and temperature distribution of the intracluster medium (ICM) of local clusters have proven pivotal for the study of cluster astrophysics. Here, we extend these measurements to $z=1.7$ with a resolved analysis of the ICM in ACT/SPT-CL J0459.6-4946. By combining high-resolution thermal Sunyaev-Zeldovich measurements using new, deep ALMA Band 1 and 3 observations, with archival X-ray data, we conclude that the cluster has (i) an ICM with a flat and relatively high ($\approx 200$ keV cm$^2$) entropy distribution out to $\approx 0.3\,r_{500,\mathrm{c}}$, (ii) a hot core ($T_{\mathrm{e}} \simeq 14$ keV) with a declining temperature profile, (iii) a short effective path length along the line of sight of $l_{\mathrm{eff}} \simeq (0.75 \pm 0.05) \times r_{500,\mathrm{c}}$, and (iv) a clumpiness factor $C = \langle n_{\mathrm{e}}^2 \rangle / \langle n_{\mathrm{e}} \rangle^2 \simeq 1.17 \pm 0.05$ within $r_{500,\mathrm{c}}$. Its dynamic nature and high redshift suggest that the cluster is still thermalising its ICM, consistent with a relatively large hydrostatic mass bias of $b = 1 - M_{500,\mathrm{c,HE}}/M_{500,\mathrm{c,WL}} = 0.27^{+0.32}_{-0.67}$ that we measure with respect to the weak lensing mass. Furthermore, a region with low entropy and high density to the south of the cluster centre is observed in the X-rays yet absent in the Compton-$y$ map, indicating pressure equilibrium; we interpret this as a sloshing cold front -- the first such detection at high redshifts. This case study demonstrates that $\approx 3$h-long ALMA observations, combined with comparatively "short" X-ray exposures ($\approx 122$ ks), can fully characterise the ICM at high redshift, opening a path towards the thermodynamics of young and distant galaxy clusters for larger samples.

title: A Composite Rest-Frame UV Spectrum of Galaxies at $5.7 < z < 6.9$: Ionization, Outflows, and Implications for Intergalactic Metal Enrichment
summary: We present a stacked JWST/NIRSpec spectrum of 104 galaxies at $λ_{\rm rest}=1200\unicode{x2013}2000\;\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ to study nebular emission and absorption from the interstellar medium (ISM) and stellar winds. The sample is drawn from known [O III] emitters with mean redshift $z=6.50$, absolute UV magnitude $M_\mathrm{UV}=-20.7$, and stellar mass $M_{\star}=10^{8.93}\;\mathrm{M_\odot}$. The stacked continuum closely resembles lower-redshift Lyman Break Galaxy composites, with a few notable differences. Ly$\;α$ has comparable strength and is redshifted relative to the [O III] systemic frame, consistent with production in gaseous outflows. High-ionization emission lines including O III], C III], and He II are slightly stronger than in lower-redshift stacks but exhibit narrow widths, disfavoring ionization from a broad-line AGN. Emission-line ratios slightly favor ionization by a hard stellar continuum, though a contribution from a narrow-line nuclear source cannot be strictly excluded. Numerous strong absorption lines at both high and low ionization are blueshifted by $\sim200\;\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, again indicating outflows driven by stellar winds or entrained metal-enriched ISM. A simple model suggests that at $z\sim6.5$ most star-forming galaxies are too young for winds at these velocities to propagate beyond $\sim3\unicode{x2013}9$ proper kpc, implying that the observed [O III] emitter population alone cannot explain the frequency of heavy-element absorbers seen in quasar spectra. In this picture, early enrichment of the intergalactic medium likely arises from undetected low-mass galaxies ($M_\star\sim10^5\unicode{x2013}10^6\;\mathrm{M_\odot}$) clustered around the more massive systems detected in JWST/NIRCam WFSS surveys.

title: Dynamically defined bulges reveal that early-type galaxies with compact bulges host more massive black holes
summary: We revisit the $M_{BH}-M_{bulge}$ relation for early-type galaxies by introducing a uniform bulge defined by dynamical decomposition. From the set of nearby galaxies with accurately measured black hole masses, we select 30 early-type galaxies that have been observed with wide-field integral-field unit instruments (MUSE, ATLAS3D, or PPAK). For each galaxy, we construct an orbit-superposition Schwarzschild model and obtain its stellar orbit distribution. In this framework, we define the bulge uniformly as comprising stellar orbits with circularity $λ_z < 0.7$ (or, in an alternative definition, $λ_z < 0.2$) and lying within $r < 3$ kpc. From these orbits, we reconstruct the spatial density distribution of the bulge and measure its mass ($M_{bulge}$), size ($R_{bulge}$) and surface density slope ($γ_{bulge}$). We find that the dynamical bulge defined by $λ_z < 0.7$ yields masses that are systematically consistent with the photometric bulge masses. Comparing to the bulge from photometric decomposition, using this dynamical bulge definition slightly decreases the scatter around the best-fitting from 0.56 to 0.47. More interestingly, we identify a clear trend: at a given bulge mass, galaxies hosting more compact bulges (i.e. smaller bulge sizes or steeper bulge density slopes) systematically contain more massive black holes; eight outliers show overmassive BHs together with ultra-compact bulges. We interpret this as direct observational evidence that the $M_{BH}-M_{bulge}$ relation evolves over a galaxy's merger history, with that history imprinted in bulge compactness. Incorporating compactness via an $M_{BH}-M_{bulge}-R_{e, bulge}$ (or $γ_{bulge}$) relation brings the outliers into agreement and reduces the overall scatter of the sample to $\sim 0.3$.

title: Introducing Aurora: A New Black Hole Seeding Model With Explicit Environmental Coupling
summary: We present Aurora, a black hole seeding module for the Mimic semi-analytic framework, in which the seed mass of each newly resolved halo is set by its environment. Motivated by evidence that early quiescent galaxies and overmassive black holes assemble in dense environments, Aurora replaces the fixed seed masses of conventional prescriptions with a continuous spectrum, coupling the seed mass to two environmental parameters, the local overdensity and the radial skewness of the surrounding haloes, and to the halo mass at seeding. Requiring only halo masses and positions, it applies to dark-matter-only simulations. Calibrated against Sage on the Millennium merger trees, this prescription leaves a lasting signal. Massive black holes are assembled from the seeds of many progenitors, seeds supplying 29 per cent of all black hole mass formed by $z=0$. A seed-dominated growth pathway, distinct from the accretion-dominated majority, emerges among galaxies assembled rapidly in dense, asymmetric environments. Environment-dependent seeding raises the quiescent fraction of seeded galaxies in massive haloes at $z \simeq 3.1$ by up to 70 per cent, with the excess concentrated in overdense environments, and a deficit in voids. Scrambling the seeding environments while preserving the mass spectrum erases this gradient. The two environmental couplings imprint separable signatures, broadening the scatter of the galaxy-black hole mass relation while preserving the stellar-halo mass relation and other Sage summary statistics. We discuss applying Aurora at gigaparsec scales and higher resolution, to understand the origins of massive black hole systems in contemporary deep surveys.
